summary: Describes using RADIUS authentication and authorization with secure SNMP Transport Models, to authenticate users and decide whether to allow secure transport sessions to be created.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets a central guard, the RADIUS server, decide who may start a secure SNMP conversation.

questions: how does radius work with snmp
what is a radius hint attribute
subtitle: How a network device uses RADIUS to decide whether a user may open a secure SNMP session over a transport such as SSH.

tldr.problem: Secure SNMP transports such as SSH check who a user is, but the traditional SSH server leaves permission to the operating system. A RADIUS database may hold many kinds of users, only some of whom should manage network devices.
tldr.mechanism: The device sends hint attributes in its Access-Request, and the RADIUS server answers with Service-Type Framed-Management, Framed-Management-Protocol SNMP and a Management-Transport-Protection value. The device must enforce them and may apply session and inactivity timeouts.
tldr.outcome: RADIUS can authenticate users and authorize SNMP sessions over secure transport models. It builds on RFC 5607 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5608 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the attributes defined in RFC 5607.

sections.title: Purpose and System Layout
sections.content:
This memo describes how SNMP secure Transport Models can use a RADIUS service to authenticate users and to authorize creation of secure transport sessions. It is generally applicable to many transport models, but its examples focus on the Secure Shell Transport Model.

Three parts are involved. A network management application talks SNMP over SSH to a network device (the managed entity). The device contains a RADIUS client and an SNMP engine, and in this document is called the NAS. The RADIUS client talks to a RADIUS server, sharing a secret with it. The RFC deliberately leaves open which internal module does what, and says the processing would quite likely sit in the secure transport module.
sections.plainLanguage: An app wants to talk to a router in private. The router phones a central guard to ask whether this person is really allowed in.

sections.title: RADIUS, Hints and Secure Transports
sections.content:
In RADIUS, a client sends an Access-Request and the server replies with Access-Accept or Access-Reject. Accept messages carry service provisioning attributes that say what service the NAS should give the user. If that provisioning does not match what the NAS can do, RFC 2865 requires the NAS to reject the access.

A RADIUS server often serves many kinds of devices and users, and usually only a small subset of users may reach the administrative interfaces of switches and routers. So the NAS commonly includes hint attributes in the request, describing itself and the service wanted. This RFC recommends the right hints for SNMP.

Secure transports like SSH do not say how to use authorization data from a AAA service. SSH servers usually integrate with RADIUS for a username and password check, often through the Pluggable Authentication Modules interface, and access control is left to the application, for example the file permissions of a Linux shell. This does not follow the usual RADIUS provisioning model.
sections.plainLanguage: A hint is like telling the guard 'I am a door on the third floor and this person wants the private chat room'. That helps the guard decide.

sections.title: Domain of Applicability
sections.content:
The credentials RADIUS needs come from the secure transport server, or in some cases directly from the SNMP engine. So the transport MUST support credentials compatible with RADIUS authentication methods: Password, CHAP, ARAP, EAP and HTTP Digest.

In practice the likely ones are Password, CHAP and possibly HTTP Digest, with Password the common denominator. Many transports support stronger methods such as public key, but RADIUS has no public key support except inside an EAP method. Because EAP is not meant as an application-layer authentication mechanism, using it here is NOT RECOMMENDED. In some cases Password may be the only compatible RADIUS method.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard only understands a few kinds of ID cards. The visitor must show one of those, even if they own fancier cards the guard cannot read.

sections.title: Authorization of SNMP Sessions
sections.content:
RADIUS gives SNMP two possible uses: service authorization and access control authorization. This RFC covers only the first; the second is described as a topic of current research. Service authorization lets the server say whether an authenticated principal may use SNMP, optionally over a secure transport. It matters because, unlike USM where every configured principal may access the device, a RADIUS back end may hold credentials for many users who should not manage devices.

The NAS MUST treat an Access-Accept that provisions a protection level or application service it cannot provide as an Access-Reject, and SHOULD treat unknown attributes the same way. The three hint attributes the NAS MUST send in the Access-Request to signal SNMP over a secure transport (authPriv) are Service-Type = Framed-Management, Framed-Management-Protocol = SNMP, and Management-Transport-Protection = Integrity-Confidentiality-Protection.

The server MUST use the same three in an Access-Accept to provision authPriv SNMP. To authorize SNMP without protection (authNoPriv), the third value is No-Protection. No combination represents SNMP noAuthNoPriv, since RADIUS always authenticates a user first.

To limit a session, the server can send Session-Timeout, the maximum seconds before unconditional disconnection, and Inactivity-Timeout, the maximum seconds without protocol activity. The NAS enforces both. The attributes themselves are defined in RFC 5607.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks 'may this person use the private line?'. The guard answers 'yes, and it must stay locked' or 'yes, an open line is fine', and can also say how long the call may last.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Threats to RADIUS use are described in RFC 3579 and RFC 3580, and SNMP security matters are in the documents for the transport subsystem (RFC 5590) and Transport Security Model (RFC 5591).

If the SNMPv1 or SNMPv2c security model is used, securityName comes from the community name; with the User-based Security Model it comes from USM. That may not be what is expected with RADIUS. Using a secure transport with RADIUS together with SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or USM is NOT RECOMMENDED. Still, the RFC says USM credentials stored locally are a useful fallback when the AAA service is unreachable, like a local root password when NIS is down.

The Message-Authenticator (80) attribute SHOULD be used. It is the best RADIUS has to give tamper-evident integrity for the provisioning attributes in an Access-Accept, and it helps protect hints in requests, since RADIUS messages are not encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages to the guard are not secret, so each one gets a tamper seal. Keeping a spare key at home is fine for emergencies when the guard cannot be reached.
